planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before the last frost in hilled, loose soil and re-hill as sprouts emerge to keep tubers covered.

directions: This mid-season variety sets oval, medium-large tubers with dark purple skin wrapped around dense golden flesh that cooks up creamy with a touch of dryness. The medium-large plants carry lavender flowers and show moderate scab resistance with only medium blight tolerance, so rotate beds and avoid overly wet soil. Space seed pieces 8-10 inches apart and hill generously, since tuber set is moderate but yields run medium-heavy under good conditions.

common_name: Prairie Blush Potato (Pink-Blushed Yukon Gold Sport)

planting.note: Plant seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; this clonal Yukon Gold sport matures only about 5 days later than its parent.

directions: Discovered as a single off-type hill growing within a planting of Yukon Gold on Wood Prairie Farm in 2001, this early-season sport was selected and stabilized for its golden skin overlaid with a distinctive pink blush. Tall-medium plants with light purple flowers produce medium-large, slightly oblong tubers with the same excellent flavor as Yukon Gold but a long dormancy that extends storage life. Give plants moderate spacing and expect medium yields with moderate resistance to blight and scab.

common_name: Baltic Rose Potato (German Red-Skinned Golden-Flesh Potato)

planting.note: Warm seed tubers before cutting and let cut surfaces heal over for a day or two before planting this late-season German heirloom.

directions: A German-bred late-season variety producing oblong, medium-large tubers with red skin over deep golden, silky flesh that fries and roasts especially well. Medium-large plants are heavy yielders and show useful resistance to potato leafhopper feeding damage in addition to moderate scab resistance. Space seed pieces about 9 inches apart in-row and allow the medium dormancy period before storage sprouting begins.

planting.note: Give this large, late-maturing russet extra elbow room at planting since it is a vigorous, heavy-setting plant.

directions: A long, brown-russeted baking potato with white mealy flesh, grown by Wood Prairie as a favorite russet that is rarely offered by other seed suppliers. Large plants with white flowers set tubers heavily, giving high yields along with very high scab resistance and strong late blight tolerance, making it a low-input choice for a long growing season. Space seed pieces 14-18 inches apart to accommodate the big plants and expect good keeping quality thanks to the long post-harvest dormancy.

common_name: French Charlotte Potato (Container-Friendly Salad Fingerling Type)

planting.note: Well suited to large containers and raised beds in addition to open garden rows; plant 4-6 weeks before last frost.

directions: A mid-season French variety popularized among organic growers, producing long-oval, medium-small golden tubers with golden, waxy-moist flesh prized for its flavor and good storage life. Medium-sized plants with violet flowers set tubers heavily, though overall yield stays moderate, and the variety shows medium-high blight tolerance with moderate scab resistance. It performs notably well in containers, making it a good pick for gardeners with limited in-ground space.

common_name: Keuka Gold Potato (Cornell-Bred Northern Golden Potato)

planting.note: A robust northern-climate variety bred at Cornell; plant 4-6 weeks before last frost in well-drained soil.

directions: Bred at Cornell University, this mid-to-late-season golden potato forms oval, medium-large tubers with golden skin and golden flesh and a reputation as an easy, dependable grower in cold-winter regions. Medium plants with white flowers set a moderate-to-heavy crop of tubers, and the variety carries high scab resistance along with medium late blight tolerance. Expect heavy overall yields and good storage keeping from this reliable Northeastern selection.

common_name: King Harry Potato (Flea-Beetle and Leafhopper Resistant Potato)

planting.note: A good choice where Colorado potato beetle, leafhopper, or flea beetle pressure is high; plant 4-6 weeks before last frost.

directions: King Harry is a mid-season, roughly 90-day potato bred for unusually hairy foliage that makes it highly resistant to Colorado potato beetle, potato leafhopper, and flea beetle feeding, a major advantage for organic growers battling these pests. It forms round, white-skinned tubers with waxy, moist flesh and is a high-yielding variety under good care. Because its main strength is insect resistance rather than disease tolerance, still rotate plantings and monitor for blight in wet seasons.

common_name: Rose Gold Potato (Pink-Skinned Golden-Flesh Best Seller)

planting.note: One of the farm's best-selling varieties; plant seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost in hilled rows.

directions: Rose Gold is a mid-season potato with light red skin over golden flesh, grown on medium plants with dark pink flowers that set tubers moderately to heavily. It is marketed by its Maine grower as among the best of the red-skinned, golden-fleshed potatoes for its attractive round tubers and excellent, creamy mid-dry eating quality. High scab resistance pairs with only medium blight tolerance, so good air circulation and crop rotation help it reach its medium yield potential.

planting.note: A workhorse late-season variety good for containers as well as rows; plant 3-5 weeks before last frost.

directions: Bred as an improvement on Kennebec, Elba is a late-season white-skinned, white-fleshed potato producing large round tubers on medium-large plants with white flowers. It combines high late blight tolerance with high scab resistance, making it one of the more disease-resistant all-purpose potatoes available, and it sets a moderate-to-heavy crop that yields heavily overall. Its waxy mid-dry texture and good all-purpose cooking performance, plus its tolerance of container culture, make it a dependable workhorse choice for home gardens.

planting.note: Bred for impressive tuber set and red color retention in storage; plant seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost.

directions: Originally bred in North Dakota and further developed at the Aroostook Farm Potato Experiment Station in Maine, Red Port is an early-to-early-midseason potato with bright red skin that holds its color well in storage over white flesh. Medium plants with pink flowers set tubers moderately to heavily, giving heavy overall yields, and the variety shows moderate resistance to scab, blackspot, and shatter bruise alongside medium late blight tolerance. Its short-to-medium dormancy means stored tubers sprout relatively soon after harvest, so plan storage timing accordingly.

common_name: Sarpo Una Potato (Early Blight-Resistant Hungarian Potato)

planting.note: The earliest-maturing variety in the Sarpo blight-resistant lineup; plant 4-6 weeks before last frost.

directions: Sarpo Una, imported from Hungary's Sarvari Research Trust, is the earliest-maturing member of the Sarpo family of potatoes bred specifically for outstanding late blight resistance. Medium plants with lavender flowers produce long, red-skinned, white-fleshed tubers with moderate-to-heavy tuber set and heavy overall yields. The waxy-moist texture suits soups, stews, and salads, and it also bakes and roasts well, combining strong disease resistance with very good eating quality.

planting.note: Grow in well-draining succulent soil under filtered or partial sun, moving pots indoors before any frost risk.

directions: Garnet Lotus forms loose rosettes in a blend of forest green and deep plum, with a fine coating of silvery hairs that give the whole plant a soft, frosted look. It sends up clusters of red flowers in spring when given enough light. Let the soil dry out fully between waterings to avoid rot, since this is a soft, moisture-sensitive succulent. It tolerates low indoor light but colors up best with brighter, filtered exposure.

planting.note: Tuck rooted cuttings into well-drained soil or rock crevices in full sun and water regularly until the mat establishes.

directions: This low, trailing stonecrop carries tiny blue-toned leaves on stems that creep and spill nicely over edges, rocks, or hanging containers, then produce small white flowers in early summer. New plantings need steady watering to knit roots into the soil, but once established the mat shrugs off months of drought. It is fully frost-hardy outdoors in milder winter climates and propagates readily from broken-off stem pieces that root wherever they touch soil. Give it full sun and sharp drainage for the tightest, bluest growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted stems in full sun with sharp drainage; water in well, then taper off once established.

directions: Turquoise Tails produces upright clusters of blue-green, pine-needle-like foliage that build into a dense, architectural groundcover, topped in summer by clouds of creamy yellow flowers that draw pollinators. Give young plants regular water to spread their roots, then expect them to coast through months of dry weather once mature. It handles winter cold well outdoors in temperate climates and spreads readily to fill rock gardens or border edges. Good drainage is essential to prevent crown rot in wetter soils.

planting.note: Plant tubers early once soil has warmed since this late-season bloomer needs the full growing season to reach its huge dinner-plate blooms.

directions: Harvest Moonlight, a 2004 Swan Island introduction, is a dinner-plate dahlia producing enormous informal decorative yellow blooms up to 10 inches across on a sturdy 4.5-foot plant with attractive foliage. Because it is a late bloomer, often needing close to 120 days to flower, it rewards patient gardeners with a strong flush of large, well-formed blooms in late summer and fall. The thick, sturdy stems hold the heavy flower heads upright, making this a good choice for exhibition as well as garden display. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and stake plants early to support the eventual flower weight.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in open soil; the single open flower form makes this variety especially attractive to pollinators.

directions: Bumble Rumble is a Swan Island collarette dahlia (2001) with soft pink, raspberry-overlaid petals surrounding an unusually wide white collar that nearly reaches the petal tips, creating strong color contrast on 3-inch blooms. The open, single-flower structure of collarette dahlias makes this variety a magnet for bumble bees and other pollinators, a nice bonus for a cutting garden. Plants grow to about 4 feet with strong, upright stems and bloom prolifically through the season, though cut flowers have a shorter vase life than many decorative types, so they are best enjoyed fresh or cut just as they open.

planting.note: This reliable bloomer tolerates both hot and high-altitude climates, so plant once soil has warmed and expect continued flowering into fall.

directions: Crazy Legs is a 1990 stellar-form dahlia with narrow, twisting bronze-orange petals and a rust-toned reverse that give the 3-inch blooms a shaggy, star-like look especially useful in fall-themed arrangements. The 4-foot plant has notably clean, attractive foliage and well-proportioned stems that hold up in both garden beds and cut bouquets, with blooms lasting about five days once cut and conditioned. It is a reliably prolific bloomer reported to perform well across a range of climates, from hot California summers to cooler high-elevation gardens, often continuing to flower into late October.

planting.note: Plant in a spot with full sun to bring out the strongest coral-orange center color as blooms mature.

directions: Coral Gypsy is a 1996 Swan Island semi-cactus dahlia whose narrow, slightly twisted petals open with a yellow-tinged orange center that softens to pink toward the outer edges as the 7-inch bloom matures, giving each flower a two-tone, sunset-like effect. The 4-foot plant produces plenty of sturdy cutting stems and is especially suited to large arrangements where its unusual coloring stands out. It is a steady, average-season bloomer that responds well to deadheading and regular harvesting, which keeps new buds coming through late summer.
